newsitem.title: UK: Serbians, Croatians face criticism at Bosnia talks.
newsitem.headline: Serbians, Croatians face criticism at Bosnia talks.

text.p: The Serbian and Croatian delegations attending a major Bosnia peace conference in London this week will face sharp criticism for how they are handling their domestic affairs.

"The reception they will be getting is different from the one they got in Dayton last year," a senior Western diplomat said on Monday, referring to the talks in Ohio which produced a deal ending the 43-month war in Bosnia.

Presidents Slobodan Milosevic of Serbia and Franjo Tudjman of Croatia will not attend the Peace Implementation Conference on Wednesday and Thursday, which is due to take stock of the year-old Bosnian peace process.
Both strongmen, hard-pressed at home by popular protests against their rule, are sending their foreign ministers instead.

"Whereas in Dayton the support of Milosevic and Tudjman was seen as essential for supporting the shaky peace deal, their democratic credentials are now under increasing scrutiny," said the diplomat, closely involved in the Dayton process.
"What they will hear now is some sharp criticism -- there will be no plaudits here for them."
More than 100,000 people demonstrated on the streets of the Croatian capital Zagreb last month in protest at Tudjman's decision to close down a popular independent radio.
"Tudjman has got his country into the Council of Europe. He's behaving as though he's forgotten that freedom of the press was one of the conditions for that admittance," the diplomat said.
In Serbia, tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets over the last two weeks to protest about what they say was fraud during local elections in November.

Serbia's opposition said it had won control over 15 out of the 18 biggest Serbian cities, including the capital Belgrade. But Milosevic's ruling party overturned the election results on the grounds that there had been voting irregularities.
"Milosevic is behaving as though Serbia has decided to align itself not with Europe but with the few remaining dictatorships in the world," the diplomat said.
"Serbia is going to wind up being isolated like Ceausescu's Romania," another diplomat said. "Look around, democracy has won the day in all neighbouring countries apart from here."
"They have no hope of getting any assistance from the western world if they continue along this path."
Milosevic raised the stakes over the weekend when the police said they would no longer tolerate street protests.

Veteran Western observers in Belgrade believe that Milosevic is hoping to wear down the opposition and that the West will overlook the domestic turmoil in return for his continuing commitment to the Bosnia peace.
Both Milosevic and Tudjman were hailed as peacemakers for their role during the Dayton talks.
"Presumably Milosevic thought this gave him carte blanche to do whatever he wanted at home," the diplomat said.
"On the contrary, the election issue will now become a condition for Serbia's reintegration into the world."
A United Nations trade embargo was lifted this year to reward Milosevic for his contribution to Dayton.
But the United States has insisted on retaining an outer wall of sanctions barring Serbia from foreign capital until it improves its human rights record.

Diplomats in London and Western observers in Belgrade doubt the Serbian police will crack down on the demonstrators during the conference, where Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic will face more than 50 ministers from Europe, North America and Russia, as well as officials from the major aid agencies.
